title: Surgical Specialties: Urology, Orthopaedics, Neurosurgery and Paediatric Surgery
description: Urological conditions, fractures and orthopaedic infections, neurosurgical emergencies, and common paediatric surgical problems.

topics.title: Urology
topics.summary: BPH and urinary retention, urolithiasis, urethral stricture, and urological cancers.

notes.b: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) causes lower urinary tract symptoms in older men — voiding (hesitancy, poor stream, dribbling) and storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia); assess with IPSS, DRE (smooth enlarged prostate), urinalysis, renal function, PSA (after counselling) and ultrasound (post-void residual, hydronephrosis). Treatment: alpha-blockers (tamsulosin), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride — shrink the gland), and surgery (TURP or open prostatectomy — still common in Nigeria) for complications. Acute urinary retention: painful, palpable bladder — urethral catheterisation (suprapubic if urethral fails or stricture). Urethral stricture (post-gonococcal urethritis, trauma, instrumentation): poor stream, retention; urethrotomy or urethroplasty. Urolithiasis: renal colic (loin-to-groin pain, haematuria); non-contrast CT KUB; analgesia (NSAIDs); stones < 5 mm usually pass; larger ones need ESWL, ureteroscopy or PCNL; obstructed infected kidney is an emergency requiring drainage (nephrostomy or stent). Testicular torsion: sudden severe testicular pain in adolescents — surgical exploration within 6 hours.

Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in Nigerian men, often diagnosed at an advanced stage with bone metastases (back pain, pathological fractures, spinal cord compression); men of African descent have higher incidence and mortality. Diagnosis: DRE (hard, irregular prostate), PSA and transrectal or transperineal biopsy (Gleason score/ISUP grade group), bone scan for staging. Treatment: localised — radical prostatectomy, radiotherapy or active surveillance; advanced — androgen deprivation therapy (bilateral orchidectomy — affordable and widely used in Nigeria; LHRH agonists), plus newer agents. Bladder cancer: painless haematuria; squamous cell carcinoma linked to chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection is common in northern Nigeria (transitional cell carcinoma elsewhere, linked to smoking). Renal cell carcinoma (haematuria, loin pain, mass) and Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma — abdominal mass in young children) are other urological malignancies. Painless haematuria in adults warrants investigation for cancer.
k: Prostate cancer: commonest in Nigerian men

topics.title: Fractures and Orthopaedic Trauma
topics.summary: Fracture description and management, complications, common fractures and traditional bone setters.

notes.b: Describe fractures by site, pattern (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, segmental, greenstick in children), displacement (angulation, translation, shortening, rotation) and whether open or closed. Open fractures are emergencies: antibiotics (within 1 hour), tetanus prophylaxis, wound photograph and dressing, splinting, then debridement and stabilisation (Gustilo–Anderson classification). Principles of fracture management: reduce (closed or open), hold (casts, traction, external fixation, internal fixation — plates, nails), rehabilitate. Complications: early — neurovascular injury, compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch; fasciotomy), fat embolism (long bone fractures — hypoxia, confusion, petechiae), infection, DVT; late — malunion, delayed union, non-union, avascular necrosis (femoral neck, scaphoid), joint stiffness and post-traumatic arthritis. In Nigeria, many fractures are first treated by traditional bone setters, leading to complications such as gangrene (tight splints), malunion, non-union and chronic osteomyelitis — some needing amputation.

Fracture of the neck of femur (elderly, osteoporosis — shortened externally rotated leg; intracapsular fractures risk avascular necrosis — hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement; extracapsular — dynamic hip screw). Femoral shaft fractures (young, high-energy; significant blood loss; intramedullary nailing — SIGN nails widely used in Nigeria). Tibial fractures (commonly open; compartment syndrome). Distal radius (Colles' fracture — dorsal angulation 'dinner fork' deformity after falling on an outstretched hand). Supracondylar humerus fracture in children (brachial artery and median nerve injury; Volkmann's ischaemic contracture). Scaphoid fracture (anatomical snuffbox tenderness — risk of avascular necrosis; treat clinically even if the initial X-ray is normal). Osteomyelitis: acute haematogenous in children (Staphylococcus aureus; Salmonella in sickle cell disease) — antibiotics and drainage; chronic osteomyelitis with sequestrum and involucrum, sinuses — common in Nigeria — sequestrectomy. Tuberculosis of the spine (Pott's disease — gibbus, paraplegia).

topics.title: Neurosurgery
topics.summary: Head injury, intracranial haematomas, raised ICP, hydrocephalus, spinal injury and brain tumours.

notes.b: Traumatic brain injury (mostly motorcycle and road crashes) is graded by GCS: mild 13–15, moderate 9–12, severe ≤ 8 (intubate to protect the airway). Primary brain injury occurs at impact; management aims to prevent secondary injury from hypoxia, hypotension, raised intracranial pressure, hypoglycaemia, seizures and fever. Extradural haematoma: temporal bone fracture tearing the middle meningeal artery, lucid interval followed by deterioration, biconvex (lentiform) hyperdensity on CT — urgent craniotomy (burr hole in emergencies); excellent outcome if treated early. Acute subdural haematoma: bridging veins, crescent-shaped, often with underlying brain injury — worse prognosis. Chronic subdural haematoma: elderly, alcoholics, anticoagulated — insidious confusion; burr-hole drainage. Raised ICP: headache, vomiting, papilloedema, falling GCS, Cushing's reflex (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) and a dilating pupil (uncal herniation compressing CN III); management — head elevation 30°, adequate oxygenation, normocapnia, mannitol or hypertonic saline, and surgery.

Hydrocephalus (excess CSF with ventricular dilatation): congenital (aqueductal stenosis, spina bifida-associated) or acquired (post-meningitic — common in Nigeria, tumours, haemorrhage); infants have enlarging head circumference, bulging fontanelle and 'sunset' eyes; treated with ventriculoperitoneal shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Neural tube defects (myelomeningocele) need early closure and folic acid prevention. Spinal cord injury: immobilise the spine, protect the airway, maintain BP (neurogenic shock), imaging and surgical stabilisation or decompression when indicated. Brain tumours: gliomas, meningiomas (common in adults in Nigeria), pituitary adenomas and metastases; in children, medulloblastoma and astrocytomas in the posterior fossa; symptoms of raised ICP, seizures or focal deficits; dexamethasone reduces oedema. Spinal TB and metastatic cord compression need urgent decompression when neurological deficit progresses.
k: Sunset eyes; VP shunt or ETV

topics.title: Paediatric Surgery
topics.summary: Neonatal surgical emergencies, congenital anomalies, hernias, and childhood tumours.

notes.b: Neonatal surgical emergencies often present late in Nigeria with sepsis and dehydration. Oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula: excessive frothy saliva, choking with feeds, inability to pass a nasogastric tube (coils on X-ray); keep nil by mouth with suction, then surgical repair. Duodenal atresia (associated with Down syndrome): bilious vomiting and 'double bubble' on X-ray. Malrotation with volvulus: bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise. Hirschsprung disease: delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours, distension; rectal biopsy (absent ganglion cells); pull-through surgery. Anorectal malformations: no anal opening — colostomy then reconstruction. Abdominal wall defects: gastroschisis (bowel protruding to the right of the umbilicus without a sac) and exomphalos/omphalocele (covered by a sac, associated anomalies). Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (2–8 weeks, first-born boys): projectile non-bilious vomiting, olive-shaped mass, hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis — correct fluids first, then Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy.

notes.b: Inguinal hernias in children are indirect (patent processus vaginalis), more common in boys and premature infants, and need prompt herniotomy because of incarceration risk. Hydrocoeles (transilluminate) often resolve by age 1–2 years. Umbilical hernias are very common in African children and usually close spontaneously by 4–5 years. Undescended testis: orchidopexy by 6–18 months to reduce infertility and malignancy risk. Circumcision complications (bleeding, glans injury, meatal stenosis) from untrained practitioners are seen in Nigeria. Childhood tumours: Burkitt lymphoma (jaw or abdominal masses — chemotherapy), Wilms tumour (smooth flank mass not crossing the midline, in children 2–5 years; nephrectomy and chemotherapy), neuroblastoma (irregular mass crossing the midline, raised urinary catecholamines), retinoblastoma (leukocoria — white pupil reflex) and rhabdomyosarcoma. Burns and trauma, typhoid perforation and intussusception are also common paediatric surgical problems.

topics.title: Vascular Surgery, Amputations and Surgical Infections
topics.summary: Peripheral arterial disease, varicose veins, diabetic foot, amputation, and surgical infections such as pyomyositis.

notes.b: Peripheral arterial disease: intermittent claudication (calf pain on walking relieved by rest), critical limb ischaemia (rest pain, ulcers, gangrene); ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI < 0.9 abnormal); risk factor control, exercise, antiplatelets and statins; revascularisation (angioplasty, bypass). Acute limb ischaemia — the 6 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold) — needs urgent heparin and embolectomy. Varicose veins (valve incompetence — saphenofemoral junction) and venous ulcers (medial gaiter area; compression therapy after excluding arterial disease). Diabetic foot: neuropathic ulcers on pressure points, infection and ischaemia; debridement, offloading, antibiotics and glycaemic control. Amputations in Nigeria commonly result from diabetic foot sepsis, trauma, traditional bone setter gangrene and malignancy; levels (below-knee preferred for prosthetic function), and rehabilitation with prostheses.

Pyomyositis (tropical pyomyositis — Staphylococcus aureus abscess within large muscles like the thigh and gluteals; common in Nigeria; drainage and antibiotics). Cellulitis and erysipelas (streptococcal; antibiotics, elevation). Hand infections: paronychia, felon (pulp space infection), and flexor tenosynovitis (Kanavel's signs — flexed finger, fusiform swelling, tenderness along the sheath, pain on passive extension — urgent surgical drainage). Buruli ulcer (Mycobacterium ulcerans — painless nodule progressing to large ulcers with undermined edges; reported in southern Nigeria; rifampicin plus clarithromycin, surgery). Gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens — crepitus, rapidly spreading myonecrosis; radical debridement and penicillin). Tetanus-prone wounds need tetanus toxoid ± immunoglobulin. Hydatid disease and amoebic abscesses are other surgical infections. Principles: drain pus, debride dead tissue, give appropriate antibiotics, and control source.
